prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- As the first president-elect with a Facebook page and a YouTube channel, Barack Obama is poised to use the Internet to communicate directly with Americans in a way unknown to previous presidents. Since the election, President-elect Barack Obama has posted weekly video addresses on YouTube. Judging by Obama's savvy use of social-networking sites during his campaign and the interactive nature of his transition team's Web site, Americans can expect a president who bypasses the traditional media's filters while reaching out to citizens for input, observers say. "The rebooting of our democracy has begun," said Andrew Rasiej, founder of Personal Democracy Forum and the techPresident blog. "[Obama] has the potential to transform the relationship between the American public and their democracy." During the presidential race, Obama's campaign won praise for its innovative use of social-networking sites, including Facebook, MySpace and MyBarackObama.com, to announce events, rally volunteers and raise money. Facebook has more than 150 million active users, and the average user has 100 friends on the site, according to the company. iReport.com: Your chance to ask President-elect Obama a question . Obama has more than 1 million MySpace "friends" and more than 3.7 million "supporters" on his official Facebook page -- some 700,000 more than when he was elected in November. His campaign also has a database of almost 13 million supporters and their e-mail addresses. Transition officials hope to transform Obama's vast Web operation and electronic list of supporters into a 21st-century tool to help accomplish his goals as president. They even have a name for this ambitious effort: Obama 2.0. "Obama has invented an alternative media model," said CNN senior political analyst Bill Schneider. "In the old model, the president talks to the people on television [and] the people talk back in polls. In the new model, communication is online, and two-way." Facebook, MySpace, YouTube and Twitter didn't exist when George W. Bush took office eight years ago. But since last November's election, Obama has wasted no time embracing these online communication portals. In recent weeks he has taped weekly video addresses and posted them to YouTube, where most have been viewed hundreds of thousands of times. Obama's staffers also have stopped posting information to social-networking sites since the election, preferring to reach out to constituents through YouTube and Change.gov, the official site of the president-elect's transition team. Visitors to Change.gov can read a frequently updated blog, post their ideas on issues facing the country, and rate others' ideas. Top-rated ideas will be gathered into a briefing book and given to Obama after he takes office. "They want information going not just from them to the voters, but from the voters back to them," Democratic strategist Steve McMahon said Wednesday on CNN's "The Situation Room." "Thirteen million people pushing a button, sending an e-mail to their elected representatives, making a phone call, taking action, is a powerful, powerful lobbying tool." "It's a very smart use of the Internet, to get people to offer ideas," said David All, a Republican Internet strategist. All hopes that Obama and his staff take a similar approach to WhiteHouse.gov, the president's official Web site. The current WhiteHouse.gov site, operated by the Bush administration, contains few interactive features. A statement on the president-elect's transition site says that Obama hopes to "use cutting-edge technologies to create a new level of transparency, accountability, and participation for America's citizens." It's fitting, then, that Obama's inauguration next week could be one of the most watched video events in Internet history. Rasiej expects that hordes of users will be watching online when Obama takes the oath of office, visiting WhiteHouse.gov and refreshing their browsers to capture the moment the site switches to proclaim Obama, not George W. Bush, as president. As president, Obama will likely not just rely on WhiteHouse.gov but use multiple Internet sites and technological tools to build grass-roots support for his agenda, observers say. "[Obama] is using the tools that are available to him today," All told CNN. "The next president will be using some of the same tools, and also some tools that haven't been invented yet."

Since the election, President-elect Barack Obama has posted weekly video addresses on YouTube. Given Obama’s skillful use of social-networking sites during his campaign and the interactive nature of his transition team’s website, observers say Americans can expect a president who bypasses the filters of traditional media while inviting citizens to offer input.

According to the company, Facebook has more than 150 million active users, and the average user has 100 friends on the site.

iReport.com: Your chance to ask President-elect Obama a question.

Obama has more than 1 million MySpace “friends” and more than 3.7 million “supporters” on his official Facebook page—approximately 700,000 more than he had when he was elected in November. His campaign also maintains a database containing the email addresses of nearly 13 million supporters.

Transition officials hope to transform Obama’s vast online operation and electronic list of supporters into a 21st-century tool for advancing his presidential goals. They even have a name for the ambitious effort: Obama 2.0.

“Obama has invented an alternative media model,” said CNN senior political analyst Bill Schneider. “In the old model, the president talks to the people on television [and] the people talk back in polls. In the new model, communication is online, and two-way.”

Facebook, MySpace, YouTube, and Twitter did not exist when George W. Bush took office eight years ago. Since last November’s election, however, Obama has wasted no time embracing these online communication platforms.

In recent weeks, he has recorded weekly video addresses and posted them on YouTube, where most have been viewed hundreds of thousands of times. Since the election, Obama’s staffers have also stopped posting information on social-networking sites, preferring instead to engage constituents through YouTube and Change.gov, the official website of the president-elect’s transition team.

Visitors to Change.gov can read a frequently updated blog, submit ideas on issues facing the country, and rate ideas proposed by others. The highest-rated submissions will be compiled into a briefing book and presented to Obama after he takes office.

“They want information going not just from them to the voters, but from the voters back to them,” Democratic strategist Steve McMahon said Wednesday on CNN’s “The Situation Room.”

“Thirteen million people pushing a button, sending an email to their elected representatives, making a phone call, taking action, is a powerful, powerful lobbying tool.”

“It’s a very smart use of the Internet, to get people to offer ideas,” said David All, a Republican Internet strategist.

All hopes that Obama and his staff will adopt a similar approach for WhiteHouse.gov, the president’s official website. The current WhiteHouse.gov site, operated by the Bush administration, offers few interactive features.

A statement on the president-elect’s transition website says Obama hopes to “use cutting-edge technologies to create a new level of transparency, accountability, and participation for America’s citizens.”

It is fitting, then, that Obama’s inauguration next week could become one of the most-watched video events in Internet history.

Rasiej expects large numbers of users to watch online as Obama takes the oath of office, visiting WhiteHouse.gov and refreshing their browsers to capture the moment when the site changes to proclaim Obama, rather than George W. Bush, as president.

As president, Obama will likely rely not only on WhiteHouse.gov but also on multiple Internet sites and technological tools to build grassroots support for his agenda, observers say.

“[Obama] is using the tools that are available to him today,” All told CNN. “The next president will be using some of the same tools, and also some tools that haven’t been invented yet.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about how President-elect Barack Obama plans to use Facebook, YouTube, Change.gov, and other online tools to communicate directly with Americans and encourage public participation.
counterfactuals.output:
# Obama plans digital presidency with Facebook, YouTube and Change.gov

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — President-elect Barack Obama, whose campaign transformed online organizing into a powerful political force, plans to bring many of the same tools to the White House as part of an effort to communicate directly with Americans and encourage public participation.

Obama’s transition team is using **Change.gov** as the center of that strategy. The website allows visitors to follow transition news, review the incoming administration’s priorities, share personal stories and submit ideas about issues facing the country.

The approach builds on a campaign that used e-mail, text messages and social-networking sites such as **Facebook** to reach millions of supporters, recruit volunteers and raise money.

Obama also plans to post his weekly presidential address on **YouTube**, giving Americans an online alternative to the traditional radio broadcast. Transition officials have already begun releasing videos on the platform, where viewers can watch and share them at any time.

Through Facebook and other social networks, Obama’s team can alert supporters to new announcements and direct them to government information without relying entirely on newspapers or television networks. The tools also make it possible for citizens to respond, circulate content and organize around policy proposals.

## Turning campaign supporters into participants

The challenge for the incoming administration will be converting a vast campaign network into a lasting civic community.

Change.gov invites users to describe their experiences through a feature called “Share Your Story” and offers updates on policy, appointments and transition activities. The site has also promoted online discussions in which Americans can submit questions and comments.

Obama has said he wants his administration to be more open and accessible. His digital strategy could help the White House explain policies quickly, seek public feedback and mobilize support for major initiatives.

But governing online will be more complicated than campaigning online. Presidential communications are subject to federal record-keeping requirements, security concerns and rules governing political activity. The administration will also face the task of sorting through potentially enormous volumes of public comments.

## A broader shift in presidential communication

Presidents have long adopted new technologies to reach the public, from Franklin D. Roosevelt’s radio addresses to John F. Kennedy’s televised news conferences. Obama’s use of online video and social media represents another step in that evolution.

The strategy is unlikely to replace traditional media or face-to-face political organizing. Instead, advisers see digital platforms as additional channels through which the president can explain decisions and invite Americans into the political process.

For supporters accustomed to receiving campaign updates on their phones, watching speeches online and organizing through Facebook, the transition’s message is clear: Election Day may be over, but the online network built during the campaign is expected to remain active.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a January 2009 news report examining “Obama 2.0,” including his campaign’s social-media success, weekly YouTube addresses, 13-million-person email list, and plans to make WhiteHouse.gov more interactive.
counterfactuals.output:
**Obama 2.0: Digital Campaign Heads for the White House**  
*By Staff Writer | January 2009*

**WASHINGTON** — Barack Obama’s presidential campaign used Facebook, text messages, online video and email to build an unprecedented political network. Now, as he prepares to take office on Jan. 20, the president-elect is trying to bring that digital operation into the White House.

The effort—sometimes described as “Obama 2.0”—aims to make the presidency more open and interactive while maintaining contact with the millions of supporters who helped elect him.

Obama’s campaign collected email addresses from an estimated 13 million people, allowing it to solicit donations, recruit volunteers and rapidly distribute messages without relying on traditional news organizations. Supporters also organized through My.BarackObama.com, while the campaign amassed large followings on Facebook and other social-networking sites.

Online video was another central tool. Since the election, Obama has delivered weekly addresses on YouTube, adapting the traditional presidential radio address for an audience increasingly accustomed to getting news on demand. The videos have allowed the transition team to speak directly to viewers and share the addresses through blogs, email and social networks.

Obama aides say they want to carry that approach into government. Plans for a revamped WhiteHouse.gov include more video, searchable information, policy explanations and opportunities for citizens to comment or participate. The transition’s Change.gov website has already tested some of those ideas by posting policy material, inviting questions and soliciting personal stories.

Moving from campaigning to governing, however, presents legal and practical complications. White House communications are subject to federal record-keeping requirements, security rules and restrictions that do not apply to a political campaign. Officials must also determine how, or whether, the campaign’s 13-million-person email list can be used once Obama becomes president.

There are broader questions about what online participation will mean in practice. Interactive websites can gather public opinion, but they do not guarantee that comments will influence policy. Heavy reliance on digital communication may also exclude Americans without reliable internet access.

Still, Obama’s operation has already changed expectations. Franklin Roosevelt mastered radio and John F. Kennedy television; Obama enters office as the first president whose political rise was inseparable from social media.

The test for “Obama 2.0” will be whether tools built to mobilize supporters can also help a president inform—and listen to—the country.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how Barack Obama’s innovative use of the Internet could transform the relationship between the presidency and the American public. Use quotes from political analysts and digital strategists.
counterfactuals.output:
Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign suggested that the Internet could turn the presidency from a largely one-way institution into a continuing network of communication, organization, and participation.

- **A direct relationship with citizens.** Email, social networks, online video, and later WhiteHouse.gov allowed Obama to communicate without relying entirely on television networks or newspapers. Media entrepreneur Arianna Huffington captured the Internet’s importance bluntly: **“Were it not for the Internet, Barack Obama would not be president. Were it not for the Internet, Barack Obama would not have been the nominee.”** The same tools could let a president explain policies directly, respond quickly to criticism, and maintain contact with millions of supporters after Election Day.

- **Citizens as participants, not merely an audience.** My.BarackObama.com—usually called MyBO—allowed supporters to create groups, organize events, contact voters, and raise money. Internet scholar Clay Shirky observed that **“the Obama campaign understood that their role was to convene their supporters, but not to control their supporters.”** Applied to governing, that model could invite citizens to discuss proposals, submit questions, volunteer in their communities, and pressure Congress rather than simply listen to presidential speeches.

- **A permanent grassroots organization.** Obama’s enormous email list and online volunteer network could be converted into support for legislation and public initiatives. Digital strategist Joe Rospars, who directed the campaign’s new-media operation, emphasized that online activity was integrated with traditional organizing rather than treated as a separate virtual campaign: **“We didn’t think of it as an Internet campaign. We thought of it as a campaign that used the Internet.”** In office, that approach could connect presidential messages to concrete actions such as town halls, calls to legislators, donations, and local service projects.

- **Broader access to political influence.** Small online donations reduced dependence on a limited group of major donors. The same logic could make presidential politics more responsive to large numbers of ordinary citizens. Marc Andreessen, the technology entrepreneur and political observer, called Obama’s operation **“a great demonstration of the power of the Internet in the hands of a political organization.”**

The transformation, however, would not automatically be democratic. Direct communication can bypass journalistic scrutiny; data collection and microtargeting can threaten privacy; and online consultation may become symbolic if officials ignore unfavorable responses. Obama’s innovation therefore created both an opportunity and a test: the presidency could become more open, participatory, and continuously connected, but it could also use digital tools to manage and mobilize public opinion more effectively.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

## Obama’s Online Dialogue Redefines Presidential Communication

As Barack Obama prepares for his upcoming inauguration, his transition team is demonstrating that the new administration intends to communicate with Americans differently from its predecessors. Rather than relying almost exclusively on speeches, press conferences, television interviews, and newspaper coverage, Obama has built an online model designed to encourage participation as well as distribute information.

The traditional presidential media model is largely one-way. The White House makes an announcement, reporters interpret it, and the public receives the news through television, radio, or print. Although journalists can question officials and citizens can write letters or contact representatives, most Americans have little direct involvement in the daily communication surrounding a presidency.

Obama’s model adds a second direction to that flow. During the campaign, his organization used Facebook and MySpace to build communities of supporters, YouTube to distribute speeches and campaign videos without the limits of television schedules, and Twitter to send rapid updates. These platforms allowed people not only to receive messages but also to share them, comment on them, organize events, and connect with other supporters.

That approach has continued during the transition through Change.gov. The website offers news about appointments and policy priorities, but it also invites citizens to submit questions, share personal stories, and discuss important issues. Online features such as public question-and-answer forums create at least the possibility of a continuing conversation between the administration and the electorate.

The distinction is important. In the traditional model, major media organizations act as gatekeepers, deciding which presidential statements deserve attention and placing them in context. In Obama’s online model, the president can speak to millions of people directly. At the same time, citizens can respond immediately and publicly, turning a presidential message into a broader discussion.

This does not mean that newspapers, broadcasters, or the White House press corps will become irrelevant. Professional reporting remains essential for independently examining presidential claims and asking questions an administration may prefer not to answer. Nor does online participation guarantee that every comment will be read or influence policy. A website can invite dialogue while still functioning primarily as a tool for publicity and political organization.

Nevertheless, Obama’s use of Facebook, MySpace, YouTube, Twitter, and Change.gov represents a significant shift in presidential communication. His upcoming inauguration will be covered through the familiar television networks and newspapers, but it will also be watched, discussed, linked, and shared across online communities.

The result is a hybrid media presidency: part traditional broadcast institution and part interactive network. Whether Obama can turn digital engagement into genuine public influence remains uncertain, but he has already changed what Americans may expect from communication with the White House.

# Obama takes digital campaign playbook to the White House

**The president-elect’s team promised to turn online enthusiasm into a more transparent, participatory government. The transition showed both the potential—and the limits—of governing through the Web.**

**WASHINGTON** — Barack Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign did more than use the Internet to raise money and recruit volunteers. It treated millions of supporters as participants in a political network—people who could organize neighborhoods, host events, share videos and receive instructions directly from the candidate.

After Election Day, Obama faced a more difficult technological test: Could the machinery that helped win a campaign be adapted to running a government?

The transition team’s answer began with **Change.gov**, a website launched days after Obama’s victory. It offered policy details, transition updates, job applications and a prominent invitation for Americans to “share your vision.” The site represented an early effort to build a digitally engaged administration around four themes that had defined the campaign: transparency, grassroots organizing, citizen input and direct communication.

“We have to use all the avenues available to communicate with the American people,” Obama said during the transition, repeatedly describing technology as a way to make government more open and accessible.

But the shift from campaign innovation to public administration immediately exposed tensions. Campaigns can move quickly, speak with one voice and collect information from supporters. Governments must follow federal law, protect sensitive material, preserve official records and serve citizens who may not support the president.

The transition, therefore, became an experiment in how far Internet politics could travel once its candidate entered the White House.

## A digital front door for the transition

Change.gov was designed as more than a static collection of press releases. Visitors could read Obama’s agenda, watch videos, submit questions and apply for positions in the incoming administration.

The “Open for Questions” feature allowed users to submit and rank questions for the transition team. Tens of thousands participated, elevating topics ranging from the economy and health care to civil liberties and marijuana policy.

The format resembled the voting systems used on social media and community-news sites. Instead of relying exclusively on journalists or political leaders to decide what should be asked, the platform gave users a role in setting the agenda.

That did not mean the public was making policy. Transition officials selected which questions to answer, and the popularity of a question did not guarantee action. Still, the exercise offered a glimpse of a government seeking structured public feedback on a national scale.

The site also published information about meetings between transition officials and outside organizations. The disclosure policy was promoted as an effort to reduce the secrecy surrounding the traditional parade of interest groups seeking influence over a new administration.

Yet the initiative also highlighted the difference between posting information and providing full transparency. Summaries could show that a meeting occurred without revealing every participant, argument or commitment. Open-government advocates welcomed the new disclosures but pressed the team to release information in searchable, reusable formats and to make transparency a routine practice rather than a temporary feature.

## From campaign volunteers to a governing network

Obama’s campaign assembled one of the most sophisticated digital organizing operations in American politics. Its My.BarackObama.com platform—known as MyBO—allowed supporters to create profiles, form groups, organize events, contact voters and raise money.

The system helped blur the line between a centrally managed campaign and a decentralized social movement. Headquarters supplied technology, voter data and broad strategic goals. Volunteers carried out much of the work locally.

After the election, supporters debated what should happen to that network. Some wanted it to remain independent and pressure the new president from the outside. Others believed it should become an organizing arm capable of promoting the administration’s agenda.

The eventual answer was **Organizing for America**, housed within the Democratic National Committee. It sought to keep Obama’s email list and volunteer network active, initially focusing on priorities such as the economic recovery plan and health care reform.

The decision gave the administration access to a ready-made national organizing base. Emails, text messages and online tools could quickly direct supporters to call lawmakers, attend events or explain policy proposals in their communities.

But moving the network into the party structure raised questions about its purpose. Was it a grassroots organization capable of challenging the administration, or a top-down operation designed to mobilize support for decisions already made?

That tension would become one of the central questions of digital-age politics. The same technology that empowers individuals can also give political institutions an unprecedented ability to identify, segment and activate supporters.

## Direct communication without the traditional filter

Obama’s team also brought the campaign’s emphasis on online video into the transition.

The president-elect delivered weekly addresses on YouTube, reviving the traditional presidential radio address in a visual, on-demand format. Americans no longer had to tune in at a particular time or wait for television news to replay selected excerpts. They could watch the full message online, embed it on a blog or share it through email and social networks.

The incoming administration framed that approach as an expansion of public access. It was also a way to bypass traditional media filters.

Presidents have always tried to speak directly to the public, but digital platforms lowered the cost and increased the speed of doing so. A White House could publish speeches, photographs, policy documents and video without depending on newspapers or television networks for distribution.

The first WhiteHouse.gov site under Obama emphasized this model. It featured a blog, policy pages, videos and links to executive actions. The administration also expanded its use of email, social media and online town halls.

Direct communication, however, is not the same as independent scrutiny. A White House video presents the administration’s preferred message. It does not automatically include opposing evidence, skeptical questioning or the context provided by reporters and outside experts.

The administration’s digital strategy therefore carried a dual identity: It could make presidential communication more accessible while also strengthening the White House’s ability to manage its own narrative.

## Transparency as policy—and promise

Obama entered office pledging a “new era of open government.” On his first full day as president, he issued memoranda on transparency and open government and on the Freedom of Information Act.

The administration said agencies should operate with a presumption of disclosure and use technology to increase participation and collaboration. It also moved to post information online that had often been difficult for ordinary citizens to locate.

Among the most visible projects was **Recovery.gov**, created to track spending under the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act. The site was intended to show where stimulus money was going, which projects were receiving funds and how those projects were performing.

The idea was politically and technologically significant. Rather than asking citizens to trust a summary from Washington, the administration aimed to provide data that journalists, watchdog groups and the public could examine themselves.

The White House also promoted **Data.gov**, a central repository for federal datasets. The initiative reflected a broader view of transparency: Government should not merely publish finished reports; it should release underlying data in formats that software developers, researchers and citizens could analyze and repurpose.

In theory, a developer could turn federal data into a map, a local search tool or a public-service application the government had not thought to build.

In practice, the usefulness of such efforts depended on the quality and completeness of the data. Datasets could be outdated, poorly documented or difficult to compare. Agencies varied widely in their technical capacity and willingness to release information.

Open-government advocates argued that posting large quantities of material online should not become a substitute for answering difficult questions, complying promptly with records requests or disclosing politically sensitive information.

## Citizen input meets the machinery of government

The transition’s experiments in public participation continued after the inauguration. The administration used online town halls, public-comment platforms and social media to solicit ideas and questions.

The appeal was clear. Federal rulemaking and policy consultation have long included formal opportunities for public comment, but those processes are often difficult to navigate and dominated by lawyers, corporations and organized interest groups. Digital tools could lower the barriers to entry.

A citizen could watch a policy presentation, submit a question or comment on a proposal without traveling to Washington or belonging to a major organization.

But broad participation created practical problems. A popular online question might reflect intense enthusiasm from a particular community rather than the priorities of the country as a whole. Organized groups could flood a platform. Duplicate comments could overwhelm agencies. And many Americans still lacked reliable broadband access or the digital literacy needed to participate fully.

There was also the question of what happened after citizens clicked “submit.”

For online engagement to be meaningful, participants needed to know whether their input changed a proposal, influenced a decision or was simply collected. Without that feedback loop, digital participation risked becoming symbolic—a modern suggestion box with no visible path to policy.

## The challenge of governing at campaign speed

The campaign’s technology operation had benefited from a single overriding objective: elect Obama. The federal government had thousands of missions, millions of employees and computer systems that ranged from modern to decades old.

Federal websites had to meet security, accessibility, privacy and records-management requirements. Officials had to determine whether comments posted on social networks constituted government records. Agencies needed to protect personal information while also making data available to the public.

The administration’s reliance on commercial platforms created another complication. YouTube, Facebook and other services could reach enormous audiences, but they were private companies with their own rules, advertising models and data-collection practices.

If presidential communication moved onto those platforms, critics asked, what happened to citizens who did not want to create accounts or allow companies to track their activity?

The White House tried to balance reach with public responsibility by posting material on government sites as well as commercial networks. Even so, the relationship between public communication and privately owned digital infrastructure remained unresolved.

## A lasting change in presidential politics

Obama’s transition did not create every tool associated with digital government, and it did not fulfill every promise of openness. But it accelerated a shift in expectations.

Citizens increasingly came to expect immediate access to presidential remarks, searchable government data, online petitions and opportunities to interact with officials. Campaign supporters expected organizing networks to remain active between elections. Journalists and watchdog groups expected agencies to release information in digital form rather than bury it in paper files.

The transition also demonstrated that technology could not, by itself, resolve political conflicts.

A website could show where recovery money was spent, but it could not settle arguments over whether the spending was wise. An online forum could identify popular questions, but it could not guarantee consensus. A social network could mobilize supporters, but it could not erase the differences between campaigning, lobbying and governing.

Obama’s central digital gamble was that the participatory energy of the 2008 campaign could be redirected toward public administration. The early transition offered evidence that government could communicate faster, disclose more information and invite broader participation.

It also revealed a harder truth: The Internet can open doors to government, but institutions still decide what happens after citizens walk through them.
